newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Wiesenthal says Swiss funds should aid E.Europeans.
newsitem.headline: Wiesenthal says Swiss funds should aid E.Europeans.

text.p: Funds from a charitable foundation proposed by Switzerland's government should go first to Eastern Europe's former Nazi victims, Simon Wiesenthal said in a newspaper interview published on Saturday.

"Many of these people freed from concentration camps came home and were locked up by the Communists. They went from one type of slavery to another -- these people should be compensated first," the Nazi-hunter told Neue Zuercher Zeitung.
Wiesenthal said he made his demand to Swiss foreign minister Flavio Cotti.
The proposed 7.0 billion Swiss franc ($4.6 billion) "Solidarity Foundation" must still gain final government approval, and pass a public referendum.
The idea for setting up the Foundation followed strong criticism of Switzerland's role in World War Two, led in part by the World Jewish Congress (WJC).
Wiesenthal, 88, was liberated from Austrian concentration camp Mathausen in February 1945 and went on to hunt down Nazis throughout the world. He still works in an office in Vienna.
WJC president Edgar Bronfman Sr has campaigned to force Swiss banks to publish records on Holocaust-era accounts. They recently complied, publishing a partial list on July 23.

Wiesenthal, who has criticised the WJC in the past, said in the interview that the "World Jewish Congress is not called the Jewish World Congress. One might think that they (the WJC) speak in the name of all Jews. That is not the case."

He added that the Nazis "did not only murder six million Jews. They also annihilated 95 percent of our elite. The Jews are unfortunately leaderless." He added it might take "generations" to build up a Jewish elite once again.
He added Jews previously had had "an aristocracy of the intellect. That is hard to trade in for an aristocracy of money. That is our tragedy."
